title: Driveway Stain Removal Brisbane: Oil, Rust & Tyre Marks | WSI
meta: How to remove oil, rust and tyre marks from a Brisbane driveway: what works, what to avoid, when stains won't fully lift, and when to call a pro.
h1: Driveway Stain Removal in Brisbane: Oil, Rust and Tyre Marks
answer: Most driveway stains in Brisbane are oil, rust or tyre rubber, and each needs a different treatment. Fresh oil lifts best when it is blotted straight away and degreased before pressure washing. Rust needs a rust remover, not more pressure. Tyre marks usually come off with a degreaser and an even surface-cleaner pass. Old oil that has soaked deep into porous concrete may fade rather than disappear, so test a small area first and keep the wash water out of the stormwater drain.

body.h: Why driveway stains get worse over a Brisbane summer
p: December is hard on driveways. Heat softens oil drips and tyre rubber so they press deeper into the concrete, summer storms wash garden soil and leaf litter across the surface, and the shaded strips beside fences and garden beds stay damp long enough for algae to take hold on top of the stains.

Add Christmas visitors, a trailer or boat parked for the holidays and more short trips in and out, and a driveway that looked fine in spring can look patchy by New Year. The good news is that most stains respond well to the right treatment, as long as you identify what you are dealing with first.
Different stains need different chemistry. Pressure alone is rarely the answer, and the wrong product can leave a worse mark than the stain.
list: Oil and grease: dark, often shiny when wet, spreading out from where a car or mower is parked. Fresh drips are easiest; old patches are often a dull grey-black halo.
Rust: orange-brown marks, usually near irrigation lines and sprinklers fed by bore water, metal pot plant bases, outdoor furniture or a steel trailer jockey wheel.
Tyre marks: black arcs where cars turn or brake, worst on new or light-coloured concrete and on hot days.
Organic growth: green, grey or black film in shaded areas. This is algae, mould or lichen, and it makes the surface slippery. Our guide to mould, lichen and algae explains the difference.
Leaf and timber tannins: brown or orange shadows under trees and timber decks, often mistaken for rust.

body.h: Fresh oil spills: what to do in the first hour
p: The faster you act, the less oil soaks in. Cement Concrete & Aggregates Australia (CCAA) recommends soaking up spills with absorbent material rather than wiping, because wiping spreads the oil and drives it further into the surface.
list: Blot the spill with paper towel or rags, or cover it with an absorbent such as cat litter, and leave it to draw the oil out.
Sweep up and bag the absorbent. Do not hose it into the garden or the street.
Apply a concrete degreaser to the remaining mark, following the label, and scrub with a stiff brush.
Rinse with as little water as you can, and collect the dirty water rather than letting it run into the gutter.
after: If a shadow remains, that is normal. The rest usually comes out with a professional degreaser pre-treatment and a surface-cleaner pass.

body.h: Old oil stains: why some will only fade
p: Concrete is porous. Oil that has sat for months or years can travel well below the surface, where neither detergent nor pressure can fully reach it. CCAA's data sheet on removing stains describes using a poultice for stubborn stains: a cleaning chemical mixed into an absorbent paste, left on the stain so it can draw the contaminant out, then removed and the area rinsed. It may take more than one application.

Professionals combine a degreaser pre-treatment with time for the product to work and an even pressure pass. On deep, old stains the honest outcome is often a big improvement rather than a perfect result. A good contractor will tell you which to expect before you book. At WSI, we flag on the written quote whether a stain is likely to lift completely or only partially.

body.h: Rust stains: a rust remover, not more pressure
p: Rust is a chemical stain, so blasting it with high pressure mostly just etches the concrete around it. The usual approach is a proprietary rust remover suited to concrete, applied after brushing off any loose rust, then rinsed thoroughly. Always test it on a small, hidden area first, because some products can lighten coloured concrete or affect exposed aggregate.

One exception: if the rust is coming from inside the slab, for example along a crack or as a bleeding spot from reinforcing steel, CCAA's guidance is to seek professional advice. That is a structural issue to look at, not just a cleaning job.
To stop rust coming back, move metal pot bases onto plastic feet, and check whether sprinklers are spraying bore water onto the driveway.

Tyre marks are rubber and oil residue baked onto the surface by heat. A degreaser pre-treatment followed by a rotary surface cleaner usually removes them. A surface cleaner keeps the nozzle at a fixed height and spins it in overlapping passes, which avoids the zebra stripes you get from a hand wand held at different distances.

The same pass lifts the general grime, so the whole driveway ends up an even colour rather than having clean patches where the stains used to be. CCAA makes the same point: a cleaned area can look different from the concrete around it, so it is often better to treat the entire surface.

body.h: DIY mistakes that make stains worse
p: We often get called after a weekend attempt has gone wrong. The most common problems are:
list: Holding a narrow pressure tip too close, which etches lines into the concrete and exposes the stones.
Using acid or strong household chemicals on coloured, stamped or exposed aggregate concrete without a test patch.
Mixing cleaning products. Some combinations release toxic fumes.
Washing oily water, degreaser or soap into the street gutter. Brisbane City Council lists driveway cleaning runoff washed into road gutters or drains as a water pollution issue residents can report.
Spot cleaning only the stain, which leaves a pale patch that looks worse than the original mark.

body.h: How WSI handles a driveway stain job
p: Every driveway is quoted on what it is made of and what is on it. A typical job looks like this:
list: Surface check: broom-finish concrete, exposed aggregate, stamped or coloured concrete and pavers each need different pressure and products.
Stain pre-treatment: oil, rust and tyre marks are treated with the right product and left to work for 5 to 10 minutes before the main pass.
Surface-cleaner pass: overlapping passes with a rotary surface cleaner for an even finish.
Edges and detail: expansion joints, edges, drains and the base of walls are finished by wand.
Drain protection and rinse: we protect drains and rinse to clean run-off.
Optional extras for pavers: dry joint sand brushed back in after the clean, on request.
after: Sealing is a separate trade. If you want the driveway sealed afterwards, we can recommend a coatings specialist. Sealing pays back fastest on exposed aggregate and on driveways where cars or work utes regularly drip oil.
For pricing, see our guide to driveway pressure washing costs in Brisbane, which explains the per-square-metre rates and stain surcharges.

body.h: How to keep the driveway clean after the holidays
list: Put a drip tray or a piece of cardboard under any car, mower or trailer that leaks, and get the leak fixed.
Deal with spills on the day using the steps above.
Sweep regularly, especially under trees, so leaves do not sit on the concrete and leave tannin marks.
Consider sealing after a professional clean if oil is a regular problem.
Book a pressure clean when the surface starts to look patchy or feel slippery. For most Brisbane homes that is every 12 to 18 months, closer to 12 months under trees.

faq.q: Can oil stains be completely removed from a concrete driveway?
faq.a: Fresh and recent oil stains usually lift with a degreaser pre-treatment and a pressure pass. Old oil that has soaked deep into porous concrete may only fade. A professional should tell you before the job whether to expect a full or partial result.

faq.q: Will pressure washing alone remove rust stains?
faq.a: Usually not. Rust is a chemical stain, so it needs a rust remover suited to concrete, tested on a hidden area first. More pressure mainly etches the concrete around the mark. Rust bleeding from inside the slab needs professional advice.

faq.q: Can I wash driveway cleaning water into the street drain in Brisbane?
faq.a: You should not. Brisbane City Council lists driveway cleaning runoff washed into road gutters or drains as a water pollution issue that can be reported to Council. Collect the dirty water or let it soak into a lawn area, and keep degreaser and soap out of the drain.

faq.q: Can tyre marks be removed from exposed aggregate or coloured concrete?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases, but these surfaces need lower pressure and a gentler, product-led approach to protect the stones and the colour layer. Always test any chemical on a small hidden area first.

faq.q: Should I seal my driveway after stain removal?
faq.a: Sealing is optional. It slows re-soiling and helps the surface resist oil and rust, and it is most worthwhile on exposed aggregate and driveways with regular oil drips. It is a separate trade from cleaning.

faq.q: How often should a Brisbane driveway be pressure cleaned?
faq.a: For most Brisbane homes, every 12 to 18 months. Driveways under trees need it closer to every 12 months because of leaf litter and tannin stains, while driveways in open sun with no oil drips can often go longer.
